## Why this one

The illustrated approach earns its title — the drawings do real work, not
decoration. Binary search, big-O, and the graph chapters land faster than in
denser texts because every idea gets a picture before the code.

## Standouts so far

- **Big-O by feel** — the runtime chapter builds intuition before notation.
- **Graphs** — BFS/Dijkstra explained with worked, drawn examples.
- **Dynamic programming** — the grid framing finally made it click.

More notes as I finish the back half.

[herdr](https://herdr.dev/) is a game changer! I’ve tried [tmux](https://tmux.app/), [Zellij](https://zellij.dev/), some homemade terminal multiplexers, and workspaces like [cmux](https://cmux.com/), but nothing helped me stay focused on what I was doing quite like herdr. Now it’s on every machine I use.

 Not saying the others are bad—they’re amazing. But after 8+ years of relying on both a mouse and keyboard, herdr saves me the mental overhead of learning more shortcuts and lets me focus on the actual task. I think it’s the future of agentic workflows!

 Currently, I use Ghostty + herdr on Mac, and Windows Terminal + herdr on Windows, both natively and through WSL.

 /btw [Terminal Multiplexers Explained, and Why You'd Use One](https://www.howtogeek.com/terminal-multiplexers-explained/)
>A terminal multiplexer is a utility that lets you "multiplex" a terminal, or use a terminal as if it were multiple terminals.
